items.title: IceWM
items.author: inatreecrown2
items.content:
IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs.

IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github.

  • Easy to use, simple and fast
  • Fully usable with keyboard
  • A large number of themes→
  • Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
  • Regenerates menus when configuration changes
  • Support for sound effects→
  • Manual placement of windows option
  • Autoraising of windows option
  • Configurable keybindings→
  • Supports DockApps in a container

IceWM is themeable. The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme, which is a collection of settings and small images. Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org. Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See .

IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there, then update.

Report your icewm bugs on Github. Only report it once and give relevant details.

Install the latest release as follows

wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
 icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
icewm-4.1.0
./configure /usr
make
make

Install from unreleased development source code

Gettext must be installed.

git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
icewm
./autogen.sh
./configure /usr
make
make

If you have cmake, an alternative is:

git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
icewm
./rebuild.sh /usr
build
make

Install package dependencies

To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script.

wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
bash  ./os-depends.sh

Verify package dependencies by:

pkg-config  x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
./rebuild.sh

More installation and configuration

IceWM is released under the terms of the GNU Library General Public License.

Contribute to ongoing development and support of IceWM by donating.

items.title: Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang
items.author: lavendermon
items.content:
are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.

“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.

One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”

The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.

Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.

Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kressinterim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.

It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.

One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.

Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”

Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

items.title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
items.author: sroussey
items.content:
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.

On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.

This release addresses those constraints in four ways:

What Edge0-145B makes possible
Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware.A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s.
Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks.Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show.
A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions.The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs.
Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence.Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money.

We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.

How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer

Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power

Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.

Reported Edge0-145B result
Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server.
Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins.
Generates faster than a person reads.
Approximately 120W typical powerSustains operation without throttling in the reported setup.
Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work.

Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.

On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards.

Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small

Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.

Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.

Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.

Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.

Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design

We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.

Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.

Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.

Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand.

Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate.

Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing.

Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency.

What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer

Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work.

Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models

Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following:

  • It scores , ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4.
  • It scores , close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3.
  • It scores , ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5.

Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations.

Scores are percentages; higher is better. A dash means no public score is available, rather than a score of zero.

Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from Edge0's internal evaluations. Claude-Opus-4.6 has no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. For Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation; HLE, GPQA, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis.

The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE. The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively.

DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report.

Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint

Edge0-145B combines a 72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop.

Mean across six benchmarksMemory footprint \(measured or estimated\)

The means cover DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, HLE, GPQA-Diamond, IFBench, and AA-LCR. Edge0 memory figures are measured internal peaks. Asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment and remain to be measured. Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score.

[Figure: Quality versus peak memory, with 48GB laptop and 64GB workstation capacities marked. Lower memory and higher scores are better; the chart's vertical axis does not start at zero.]

Local agents that plan, code, run, and check their work

A single natural-language request can start an entire local workflow. Edge0-145B breaks down the requirements, plans the steps, writes code, and calls tools to run it. When something fails, it debugs and repairs the code. It then takes screenshots to inspect the result and keeps iterating until the work is complete.

These projects often take dozens of rounds of planning, execution, and review. Local inference means those additional conversations, code revisions, and visual analyses incur no corresponding cloud-model token or API charges. Code and data can stay on the computer, and core model capabilities work offline.

Video production: generating Tesla's Roadster explainer within an hour

Edge0-145B produced an explainer about how Roadster could fly, handling technical research, scriptwriting, asset generation, and editing. We asked it to make the principles understandable to a general audience. The model ran locally without cloud-model calls or cloud token consumption, avoiding network round trips for inference.

The video was generated within an hour. Producing comparable work manually would have taken a director and scriptwriter, a 3D modeler, an editor, and a physics expert a month. An AI video workflow could previously cost more than hundreds of dollars; local inference eliminates the corresponding cloud-model token and API fees.

3D modeling: a Manhattan city scene in Blender

Edge0-145B built a 3D scene of Manhattan within an hour. Working in Blender from text and reference images, it constructed the scene, adjusted materials and lighting, and iterated on the rendered output.

The workflow brings visual inspection, code generation, and revision together inside Blender. The model works with objects, spatial relationships, and the creative goal, going beyond the pixels in a reference image. It inspects the result, writes code, and makes changes without handing those steps back to a person. The entire process stays local.

Creating a Manhattan-scale city scene manually would typically cost approximately and take at least a month. A leading cloud model would still incur more than $150 in cloud token charges. Edge0-145B completes the local inference without those cloud-model token fees.

Game development: playable games and a medieval city

Edge0-145B can create playable games locally. We also used its 3D modeling capabilities to build an original medieval capital for a fantasy RPG and render a at game-trailer quality.

The model planned the city independently and built it from scratch in Blender: city walls, more than a thousand old-town homes, a plaza fountain, a Gothic twin-tower facade, a rib-vaulted nave, and stained-glass windows.

The fixed camera path made errors visible. Geometry clipping, occlusion, or incorrect proportions would appear along the route, so the model inspected the renders and corrected its work as it built. The workflow ran entirely locally.

A leading cloud model required hundreds of tool calls and hundreds of millions of tokens for a single completion, using the same prompt, reference images, and camera route. Edge0-145B delivered it on a laptop without cloud-model token or API fees for local inference. An art team would typically spend weeks and thousands of dollars producing a city scene to this standard.

Hardware control: code that flies a real drone

Edge0-145B wrote the program for a real drone from one instruction: “Write a drone program that navigates through obstacles and finds a red backpack.”

It generated the flight-control and visual-recognition programs locally. The drone then took off indoors, navigated through a dense row of obstacle poles, searched autonomously, and located the red backpack beside a wall. The task required no human-written code and no cloud call.

Hardware developers can describe the behavior they want and have the model turn it into a program for a real device, without moving repeatedly between an editor, documentation, and debugging tools.

PCB design: from KiCad layout to an assembly animation

Edge0-145B took a PCB design from component placement through an assembly visualization. We asked it to design a board for itself. It started from scratch in KiCad, placed components, routed a two-layer board, and imported the design into Unreal Engine 5. It then set up cameras and lighting and rendered an animation of PCB fabrication and assembly.

A single computer delivered work that previously required a hardware engineer and a 3D designer to hand tasks back and forth over several days. Schematics and board layouts can stay on the team's own hardware, supporting trade-secret protection and data-handling requirements without uploading the designs to a cloud model.

Why Edge0: A Full Stack for On-Device AI

Useful on-device AI requires model development, inference engineering, and hardware adaptation to work together. Our progress rests on three capabilities: developing complementary models quickly, optimizing the full stack, and carrying lessons from each deployment into the next.

Our September release of Edge0-35B showed what that approach could deliver on a phone. Its launch post passed 1.2 million views on its first day without paid promotion in overseas communities. Researchers and technical experts at OpenAI, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and other companies shared it, and the model reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's overall Trending chart.

We released the model weights and unified inference framework together, giving companies and researchers a standard approach they could reproduce. The release helped move the discussion of on-device AI from a few billion parameters to the 35B tier.

Four Model Families for On-Device AI

Over the past year, we released 200 models across four families. Each handles a different part of the work, from listening and speaking to fast decisions, memory, and complex agent tasks.

Complex agent tasks and vibe coding145B and 120B models for laptops; 35B and 8B models for phones. The laptop models support vibe coding, while the phone models support agent tasks.
ASR-Infinite and 3B, 0.6B, and 0.1B ASR models for speech recognition; 0.6B and 0.1B TTS models for speech synthesis; and a 0.1B Chat model for end-to-end voice interaction.
0.6B and 3B models covering text, speech, and vision, with multimodal decisions in approximately 40 milliseconds.
A 0.6B multimodal embedding model for text, speech, images, video, and files, supporting local long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation \(RAG\).

The portfolio spans tens of millions to more than a hundred billion parameters. Both Edge0 and Audio8 have reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's Trending chart.

Models and Inference Systems Designed Together

We develop the model and the inference framework together, building hardware constraints into training and optimizing the engine for different chips. This connects model capability with the software and hardware needed to use it locally.

That work requires expertise in model development, inference frameworks, and low-level hardware adaptation. The combination is difficult for a company focused only on model development to reproduce.

Hardware Optimizations That Carry into Each Deployment

Each deployment gives us reusable optimizations for the next chip, model, or product. This matters because on-device hardware is fragmented: NPU architectures differ, as does support for numerical formats such as INT4, INT8, and FP4. A general-purpose model cannot automatically make full use of every chip.

We adapt to individual platforms. Our portfolio now covers 95% of mainstream chip platforms, including Qualcomm, BES, Rockchip, Allwinner, D-Robotics, and NVIDIA, across headphones, glasses, phones, PCs, and robots. This is portfolio-wide coverage; model requirements vary, and it does not mean every device can run Edge0-145B.

That deployment work now spans more than 5 million production devices. Our open-source models passed 15 million downloads within three months. By October 2026, we had more than 110,000 customer organizations.

The portfolio figures come from company papers and internal testing. They describe the broader Edge0 portfolio; the 145B performance results in this article apply specifically to Edge0-145B.

For Edge0-145B, day-one support covers macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA platforms such as RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090. The release includes one-click deployment tools and hardware guides.

The Future of On-Device AI and the Cloud

More complex work can stay on the device as local models approach cloud-level capability. Privacy, cost control, and offline access have long favored local execution; the remaining question was whether an on-device model could do the work. Edge0-145B expands the range of tasks for which it can.

Why More AI Work Can Stay Local

Local execution addresses four practical obstacles to adopting cloud-only AI:

  • Control cloud-model costs. Local inference adds no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees as usage grows.
  • Keep sensitive data local. Code, documents, and business records can stay on the hardware, giving teams control over data handling.
  • Sustain a responsive experience. Model and inference-engine design address response speed, power use, system responsiveness, and continuous operation together.
  • Keep core capabilities available offline. Local tasks continue when connectivity drops; features that depend on online information or services still need a connection.

From Cloud First to More Complex Work On-Device

We see the division of work between devices and the cloud shifting through three stages.

Before September 2026: cloud first, with on-device support. Apple Intelligence reflected this stage: it protected privacy, but handled a limited range of tasks locally while more demanding work relied on cloud capabilities.

After Edge0-35B's September 10 release: everyday tasks locally, complex tasks in the cloud. Local models could take on frequent requests that needed immediate responses. For one leading headphone manufacturer, our hybrid solution now handles 92% of AI usage on-device and 8% in the cloud. Everyday conversation accounts for most use cases on consumer wearables.

With Edge0-145B: toward on-device first, with cloud support. Vibe coding and other complex tasks can now run on a personal computer, giving teams more scope to choose local execution. This extends the range of work that can stay on the device while preserving the cloud for tasks and hardware that need it.

The diagram shows the shift from cloud-first AI to everyday local tasks and then more complex local work. Its colored areas are schematic, not measured usage shares.

Where Cloud AI Still Fits

Hardware constraints still determine which model fits. Compute capacity, heat, and battery life matter: Edge0-35B runs on phones, while Edge0-145B runs on suitably equipped laptops. A very low-compute device cannot currently run a 145B model locally. It needs a smaller model suited to its hardware or cloud access to a model of that size.

Cross-device long-term memory and searches requiring highly current information still require cloud services. Local and cloud models can work together; the appropriate split depends on the task, the hardware, and the information it needs.

The aim is to make local execution a practical choice for demanding work, with a capable model that can keep working close to the person using it. That is the next step toward our goal of enabling intelligence at zero distance for everybody.

Download the models to run locally, evaluate or fine-tune them, and build them into your own products:

For hardware or product integrations, reach the Edge0 team through GitHub or contact@autoark.ai.

items.title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
items.author: scottjg
items.content:
The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime:

My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one:

It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality.

This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep.

Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume.

The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of).

The existing Home Assistant integration#

Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant. The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà!

The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks.

Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break:

  1. Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it.
  2. Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well.
  3. Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it.
  4. Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device.
  5. Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban.

On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows).

I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server.

Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one.

All that said, two major things have changed.

First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys.

So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it.

The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes.

Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud.

Initially, I tried to set it up like this:

This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution?

The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi:

Next, we need to configure the Pi.

I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes.

Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions.

After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with:

scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset
table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8
	set client_interfaces { # handle 4
		type ifname
		elements = { "wlan0" }
	}

	chain prerouting { # handle 1
		type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept;
		meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6
	}

	chain input { # handle 2
		type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept;
		iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7
		iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8
		iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9
		iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11
		iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13
		iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14
		iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15
	}

	chain forward { # handle 3
		type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept;
		iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16
		oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17
		iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18
		iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19
	}
}
table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12
	chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1
		type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept;
		ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2
	}

	chain filter_forward { # handle 3
		type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept;
		ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5
		ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6
		iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7
		iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8
		oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9
	}
}

Basically, the rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of .

Also on the Pi, runs with its web interface, , using a command line like this:

mitmweb \
  --mode transparent --showhost \
  --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \
  --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \
  --set web_open_browser=false \
  --emudhra-old

Yes, off the shelf, has a built-in option () to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic.

Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the web interface:

So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made .

The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list.

The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all.

has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in ’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic.

Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests:

We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able.

The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices.

Going back to the in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned:

{
    "header": {
        "success": true,
        "result": "S1000",
        "message": "SUCCESS"
    },
    "payload": {
        "macAddr": "<redacted>",
        "certToken": "<redacted>",
        "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com",
        "port": 8883,
        "serial": "<redacted>",
        "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0",
        "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem",
        "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key",
        "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt",
        "svcCode": "002AIR007",
        "countryCd": "US"
    }
}

So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is.

For now, we can write another plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream:

The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now…

There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway.

When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way.

I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before. My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it, and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode.

Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C.

This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs.

Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via , look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs.

After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this:

  1. Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address.
  2. Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic :
    "P001" + protobuf {
  command: 1,
  key: Base64(random_letters)
}
  3. Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address.
  4. Build the configuration payload, which looks like this:
    {
  "cmd": 2,
  "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi",
  "pwd": "example-wifi-password",
  "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF",
  "type": 1,
  "macAddr": "112233445566",
  "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem",
  "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0",
  "certToken": "example-enrollment-token",
  "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001"
}
    That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to as well.

Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes.

The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script.

I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload ( and ). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration.

Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan.

Home Assistant integration#

Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan. My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly.

After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant.

And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home.

All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night.

items.title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
items.author: firloop
items.content:
Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence.

The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.

Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant GroupLink ↗

Chip the model was started on
NVIDIA Hopper
NVIDIA Hopper
NVIDIA Hopper

• Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported.

A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method.

  1. Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors, or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training.
  2. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint.
  3. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released.
  4. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3.
  5. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma.
  6. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars.

Table 2. Rough scale of each training runLink ↗

Blackwell GPUs, best estimate

Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5.

We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count. Two disclosed runs on the same hardware show the spread: Mistral says it trained Mistral Large 4, which has the same number of active parameters as DeepSeek-V4-Pro, on 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs, while Microsoft says it trained MAI-Base-2, a model of similar size trained on more data, on 16,000 in 38 days. At that pace the two largest runs here would have needed about 8,000 to 9,000 Blackwell GPUs. The figures cover only the final training run of each model, not experiments, earlier runs or serving.

Revised November 12, 2026. The first version of this report gave 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs for the largest runs and $150 million to $200 million for the largest cluster. Those figures assumed the GPUs ran as efficiently as NVIDIA’s own benchmarks, and training runs disclosed on Blackwell have been less efficient. The estimates above replace them. We have also added H100 equivalents and estimated run lengths.

A model’s , also called , are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point.

To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called . (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go.

illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself.

Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it.

Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. shows why only the correct combination recreates the original arrangement.

On real chips, the thread counts are much larger, but the principle is the same. In the NVIDIA configurations examined here, the Hopper H100 SXM, H200 and H800 have 132 SMs and use 270,336 threads; the Blackwell B200/B300 have 148 SMs and use 303,104 threads; and the Blackwell GB200/GB300 have 152 SMs and use 311,296 threads. Recovering the thread count therefore tells us which of these hardware groups matches the starting arrangement, although it cannot distinguish chips within a group. A Hopper match, for example, cannot tell an H800 from an H100 or H200.

The question is whether enough of that arrangement survives training for us to recover it. Some weights, such as those reserved for words or symbols never encountered during training, can remain untouched and retain their starting values almost exactly. We can compare these preserved values directly with the starting values generated by a candidate seed and thread count. shows such a comparison: DeepSeek-V3’s preserved weights match the Hopper arrangement, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s match the Blackwell arrangement.

Even weights that training has changed can retain a faint trace of their starting values. Each final weight is its starting value plus all the adjustments made during training. If those adjustments do not completely cancel or overwhelm the starting differences, some of those differences survive. For example, two weights that begin at 0.2 and 0.8 and each increase by about 0.1 will still be ordered the same way afterward. Real adjustments vary much more, so one weight tells us little. But across hundreds of thousands of weights, we can test whether higher starting values still tend to correspond to higher final values. shows this weak but measurable relationship. It is a finding in these weights, not a property guaranteed to survive every training run.

These surviving traces let us work backward. Suppose, in an invented example using Figure 1’s layout, seed 7 makes the first thread produce 0.2, −0.5 and 0.8. With 48 threads, those values go into positions 1, 49 and 97; with 40 threads, they go into positions 1, 41 and 81. If the published weights preserve the first pattern, we can try candidate seeds and thread counts until we recreate it. In the actual investigation, we compare thousands of values in their corresponding positions. Untouched weights can match exactly; trained weights may show only the weaker resemblance described above. In either case, we look for the combination that best reproduces the surviving pattern.

We then test that combination on weights we kept out of the search. Having chosen a seed and thread count using one set of weights, we use them to predict the starting values of a different set, without changing either setting to improve the fit. A match on these previously unused weights is stronger evidence than a match confined to the weights that helped us choose the combination. Figure 6 shows the comparisons: DeepSeek-V3 matches the initialization layout of Hopper H100 SXM, H200 or H800 chips; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matches Blackwell B200/B300; and Kimi K3 matches Blackwell GB200/GB300.

In our investigations, we found patterns strongly suggestive of initialization on Blackwell chips in six models from four Chinese companies: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro from Moonshot AI, MiniMax-M3 from MiniMax, and Ling-3.1-flash from Ant Group. V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the 148-SM layout; the other four match the 152-SM layout. These are fingerprints of the starting weights, which support, but do not by themselves prove, the use of Blackwell chips for training AI models.

Limits of our investigation

Notably, the forensic method we used to identify the hardware on which these models were initialized only works for certain models. It needs published weights, so closed models cannot be checked. It also needs a recognizable, hardware-dependent pattern from the software that generated the starting weights. PyTorch on the GPUs examined here leaves such a pattern; Baidu’s PaddlePaddle framework, which was used to train Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 model, does not. We were able to recover the seed for ERNIE-5.5 (2760), but could not identify which hardware was used to initialize it. Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them. We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search.

The method identifies the hardware that generated the starting weights, not every chip that later helped train the model. When a training run creates its weights on the same GPUs that will train it, the fingerprint points to both. But a lab could generate the weights on one system and move them to another, or continue training an existing model on new hardware. The weights alone cannot rule out those possibilities. A mixed cluster introduces the same limitation. If NVIDIA chips generated some weights and Huawei chips later helped train them, the NVIDIA pattern could survive without revealing Huawei’s participation. Different NVIDIA generations could leave different patterns in the parts they initialized, if those traces survived. In Kimi K3, at least 64 separately seeded processes each left the same 152-SM layout. A Blackwell-compatible pattern therefore supports its use at initialization, subject to the AMD alternative below; it does not establish that the entire training run used Blackwell. A Hopper pattern likewise does not rule out later training on Blackwell.

The weights also cannot reveal who owned the chips or where they were located. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. The evidence concerns access to the hardware; by itself, it does not establish that chips were smuggled into China or that an export-control violation occurred.

Could a different chip produce one of these Blackwell-compatible patterns? Among the NVIDIA configurations tested here, the older chips cannot: software can use fewer of a chip’s processing units, but cannot give it more than it physically has. Under the standard PyTorch behavior examined here, they cannot produce the 148- or 152-SM layouts. The China-market Blackwell graphics cards use a different number of threads per SM and do not produce either total.

AMD presents a different possibility. An MI300X normally uses 304 processing units, but it can be divided into two groups of 152 or configured to use only 148. Its random-number software can also generate the same underlying sequences as NVIDIA’s. Such configurations would be very unusual, but we confirmed on a physical MI300X that, limited to 152 or 148 of its units, it reproduces the layouts we associate with Blackwell, so the layout alone does not settle the question.

To distinguish them, we looked for small numerical differences in the values themselves. AMD and NVIDIA perform one calculation in the number-generating process slightly differently. On a physical MI300X, DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s preserved weights point to NVIDIA: in the 377 values where the two vendors’ results differ, the published weight matches NVIDIA’s in 363 and AMD’s in none. The same test could not settle the other five models, but we consider the AMD explanation very unlikely for them. In its normal configuration, an MI300X produces neither layout; a lab would have had to configure an entire cluster to use the same number of processing units as a Blackwell chip. Other public evidence also points to Blackwell: U.S. officials and press reports have alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, and Ant Group’s public code includes benchmark results generated on a GB300.

To reproduce the result that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, we ran unmodified PyTorch on a Hopper-class NVIDIA H100 and a Blackwell-class NVIDIA B300. We had identified DeepSeek’s seed number as 953049583, and found that it was used in the initialization of both DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Using that seed, the H100 reproduced the preserved starting values in DeepSeek-V3, but not V4-Flash; the B300 reproduced the preserved values in V4-Flash, but not V3. On the B300, unmodified PyTorch reproduced 461 of the 469 selected rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with correlations above 0.99, including 445 entire rows that matched bit for bit. Eight selected rows were partly changed by training. On the H100, it reproduced all 57,344 preserved values in DeepSeek-V3 bit for bit. Neither chip reproduced the other model’s preserved rows. Changing the seed by one reproduced no matching rows on either machine. On a rented GB200, unmodified PyTorch likewise reproduced all 13 of Kimi K3’s preserved rows using Moonshot’s seed, 20256586; changing the seed by one reproduced none. The code and the preserved weights needed to repeat these checks are public; the same comparison also runs without a GPU.

Our forensic method also gets the right answer when the answer is already known. There are 24 cases where a developer has publicly named the hardware behind a specific model; our forensic method agrees with every one. Meta’s Llama 3.1 models, trained on H100s, read as 132; eight of EleutherAI’s Pythia models, trained on A100s, read as 108. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of training, reads as 152, the same as Kimi K3. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for earlier models. Our Hopper readings are consistent with those disclosures, but would also be consistent with H100 SXM or H200 hardware; they do not independently verify H800 use.

When we compare the published weights with the numbers generated by a candidate seed and chip layout, some resemblance is inevitable even if the candidate is wrong. How much resemblance counts as evidence depends on how many weights we compare: agreement across a handful of numbers could easily be accidental, while agreement across thousands is much harder to explain by chance. Our statistical model accounts for the number of weights compared and measures how far the observed match exceeds the resemblance expected by chance. We express that distance in standard deviations, or . A higher score means stronger evidence against an accidental match, provided the statistical model correctly describes the random variation in the data.

We must also account for how many candidates we tried. Searching roughly six trillion combinations of seed and layout gives us trillions of opportunities to find a lucky match. Under a normal-distribution model, a positive match of five sigma or more occurs by chance about once in 3.5 million comparisons. That would be striking in a single test, but unsurprising somewhere in a search as large as ours. We therefore use approximately eight sigma as our benchmark for assessing accidental matches across the full search.

Our findings exceed that benchmark by a wide margin. We first select a seed and layout using one set of weights, and then test that same combination on a separate set that played no part in choosing it. This checks whether the apparent fingerprint extends beyond the numbers that led us to it. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma; even the weakest individual test reported reaches 20 sigma. Under our statistical model, these results are far too strong to attribute to accidental resemblance. They establish evidence of a shared initialization pattern; identifying precisely which computing hardware produced that pattern, and whether it also performed the training, requires the separate arguments discussed above.

Based on our forensic investigation, we believe that we have strong evidence that six Chinese AI models were initialized on export-controlled NVIDIA hardware, and that for DeepSeek-V4-Flash the evidence is conclusive; we believe that this initialization also strongly suggests that they trained on the same export-controlled hardware. While this leaves unanswered other questions—such as the circumstances through which the companies that developed these models acquired export-controlled NVIDIA systems—we believe that this fact deserves urgent attention from the public.
