items.title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
items.author: cybermango
items.content:
Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.

Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”

Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić. They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.

“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks, he says.

The object, called 2026 ED138, is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.

“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”

Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides. But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.)

Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet

Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions.

ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger.

Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says.

Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light.

Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.”

Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.”

The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds.

What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement.

“I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb, a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.”

Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood.

“Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.”

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
items.author: jonbaer
items.content:
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.

Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator

Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.

For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.

Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.

  • Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.

Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.

  • Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new tier.

Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.

items.title: Rust 1.100
items.author: mbStavola
items.content:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via , you can get 1.100.0 with:

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel () or the nightly channel (). Please report any bugs you might come across!

After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, ! This also completes the project goal for this work.

The never type, spelled in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as , , and , also have the type .

Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a or an :

While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:

Additionally this release changes to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used be compatible with using . This was the plan ever since the introduction of and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).

Unfortunately, to allow changing , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from to in editions 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.

We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently and . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized trait.

This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

: run a closure on every exit path

The trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we , , or panic. being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.

Implementing can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.

takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements and so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.

also implements a associated function which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:

Conjuring zero-sized types

As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.

Instead of transmuting , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.

Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.

Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo

Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every in a package when only some may use it.

Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.

A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running won't show warnings for unused because another may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.

Reducing Cargo cache collisions

Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the and then uplifts final artifacts to the . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a across git worktrees.

The now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.

This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.

We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.

Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns

Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.

When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:

When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:

The newer version will be recorded in and kept from then on until a later re-resolves it.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a field in the index are never held back.

  • ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with if needed.

  • Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.

Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

items.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
items.author: soheilpro
items.content:
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).

As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. 

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.

Specifically, the flaw exists within the function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.

According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.

The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:

Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:

  • Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version or later. This release addresses the race condition in .

  • Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than .

2. Implement Temporary Mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

  • Edit the configuration file (such as ) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:

items.title: 93% of paint splatters are valid Perl programs (2019)
items.author: zenincognito
items.content:
In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl?

We answer this question in the affirmative: it to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs.

Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. items.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
items.author: herpderperator
items.content:
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing  and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.

Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as and to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. 

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app. 

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."

"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

items.author: iamdelirium
items.content:
Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.

Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass

Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.

You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:

  • Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
  • choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
  • Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.

items.title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
items.author: mbac32768
items.content:
Published on 10 Nov 2026 by mbacarella
A war story from Jane Street's systems team: a false smoke alarm, a datacenter with no cooling, and a sprint to pull every power cord before the sprinklers went off

AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect.

Everyone’s heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didn’t do titles, and we on the systems team weren’t above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firm’s blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street.

For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feel… odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didn’t want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables.

Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didn’t exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner who’d served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you don’t trust the automation unless there’s a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off.

As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza, which was otherwise just a normal office building.

When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. I’d gone to a magnet high school in the city, so I’d been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it.

Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided I’d get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called “panty droppers”, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stone’s throw away in case there was an emergency.

And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off.

We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality they’re not quite that dumb, but it’s close.

Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually aren’t kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads don’t have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and that’s when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they don’t spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasn’t been brought under control since it’s gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water.

Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. We’re still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, there’s no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldn’t spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!)

Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands.

And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything.

I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands.

Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet I’d never heard before set in on the machine room.

The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers.

Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning.

There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but that’s a story for another day.

As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means there’s a generalized cooling failure.

What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldn’t cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if it’s elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat.

Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high.

Our team didn’t interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but I’d like to think he would have approved.

items.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
items.author: brownrout
items.content:
Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.

Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.

As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.

I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.

To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).

I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.

Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

items.title: I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
items.author: Brajeshwar
items.content:
Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.

To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.

Company representatives providing responses

Eric Sveum, PR manager

Emily Ewing, public relations manager

Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson

Chris De Maria, director of public relations

Sarah Novatt, spokesperson

Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager

Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events

One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)

As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.

Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.

Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.

1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?

No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.

Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.

If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.

Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.

Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.

No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.

The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.

Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.

Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.

No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.

However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.

Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.

For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.

If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.

Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.

No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

4. Do your TVs collect any screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching?

Apple TV 4K does not use automatic content recognition (ACR), nor does it collect screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching. If a user chooses to ask a question about what’s on their screen, that data is processed by Siri AI. This feature is only initiated by a direct user request.

Google TV platform software does not utilize Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to capture on-screen video or screenshots. (Note: Third-party TV hardware OEMs may install separate ACR software, but Google TV OS itself does not).

Hisense did not respond to ’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

No. ACR in LG TVs does not collect or store screenshots, screen images, screen recordings, or video recordings from the TV. Instead, it uses audio fingerprints generated from content audio using the TV’s internal soundboard (not a speaker) to identify the content being viewed.

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

No. Samsung TVs do not capture or store screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers watch.

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV?

Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings.

items.title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
items.author: emschwartz
items.content:
Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this .

In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.

Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself.

Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in , repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer.

The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%.

On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked.

How Astra fixed the loops#

Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way.

Finding the loop direction#

Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops.

Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called ). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$:

$$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$

So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.

Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:

$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$

At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model from looping whenever it’s used.

Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a change:

$$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$

At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes.

That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems:

Random direction (control)

Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text.

The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing.

The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything. Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours.

Choosing v is a linear program#

Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities.

I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts, and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$

In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable.

Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts.

To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero.

That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute.

I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a : label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning.

With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there.

A few other things showed up:

  • The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7.
  • Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$
  • A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model.

A steering vector does the same job#

An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way. So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token.

The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a , a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token.

The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths:

Steering strength (× the LP edit’s average push)

For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem.

At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart.

The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time.

Limitations and what’s next#

This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it.

Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece.

Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream. If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing.

Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub.
